title: Updating a factorization as the data change
text:
Many statistical calculations involve a sequence of designs that differ by only a few observations or predictors. A moving-window analysis, for example, repeatedly removes the oldest observation and includes a new one. Recomputing a factorization at every step repeats work on the part of the design that has not changed.
Updating and downdating use the existing factors to incorporate that local change. The choice of representation remains important: qrupdate() and qrdowndate() modify QR factors, whereas rupdate() and rdowndate() retain only the triangular information. The examples first examine individual insertions and deletions, where the resulting design is easy to reconstruct, before combining the operations in a repeated regression calculation.

1 Insert and remove observations
We use full factors as inputs to the QR update routines in these examples. A batch containing \(m\) new rows is supplied as a \(p\times m\) matrix U: its transpose is appended to the design. The position k is one-based; k = n + 1 appends observations.
set.seed(2027)
n <- 120L
p <- 6L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
initial <- fastQR::qr(X, complete = TRUE)
U <- matrix(rnorm(p * 3L), p, 3L)
X_added <- rbind(X, t(U))
added <- fastQR::qrupdate(
  Q = initial$Q, R = initial$R, k = n + 1L, U = U,
  type = "row", fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
removed <- fastQR::qrdowndate(
  Q = added$Q, R = added$R, k = n + 1L, m = ncol(U),
  type = "row", fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
relative_error <- function(a, b) {
  norm(as.matrix(a - b), "F") / max(norm(as.matrix(b), "F"), .Machine$double.eps)
}
row_checks <- c(
  after_insertion = relative_error(added$Q %*% added$R, X_added),
  after_deletion = relative_error(removed$Q %*% removed$R, X))
knitr::kable(data.frame(operation = names(row_checks), error = row_checks),
             digits = 16, row.names = FALSE)



operation
error




after_insertion
4e-16


after_deletion
5e-16



stopifnot(max(row_checks) < 1e-10)
Removing the same observations restores the original design, although it need not reproduce the original factor entries: signs and orthogonal completions can differ while representing the same matrix. Reconstruction therefore provides the relevant check. A downdated QR representation can also exist after a loss of rank, but a unique ordinary least-squares coefficient vector then requires additional treatment. The remaining design should be checked before its triangular factor is used in an unpivoted regression solve.


2 Insert and remove predictors
Adding a predictor changes the column space that a regression model can use. If V contains new columns, their components along the existing basis are \(Q_1^\top V\), while \((I_n-Q_1Q_1^\top)V\) contains directions not already represented by X. A column-update algorithm incorporates those components and restores a triangular factor for the enlarged design. If the residual directions are dependent, the enlarged matrix does not acquire one independent direction per new column.
The insertion position changes the order of the predictors, so reconstruction is checked against a design assembled in exactly that order. Column deletion reverses the structural change, but the returned factors need not have the same entries as the starting factors.
For columns, U has the same number of rows as the design. Here two new predictors are inserted before column 3 and then removed from those same positions.
V <- matrix(rnorm(n * 2L), n, 2L)
k <- 3L
X_wider <- cbind(X[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], V, X[, 3:p, drop = FALSE])
wider <- fastQR::qrupdate(
  initial$Q, initial$R, k = k, U = V, type = "column",
  fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
narrower <- fastQR::qrdowndate(
  wider$Q, wider$R, k = k, m = ncol(V), type = "column",
  fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
stopifnot(relative_error(wider$Q %*% wider$R, X_wider) < 1e-10,
          relative_error(narrower$Q %*% narrower$R, X) < 1e-10)


3 Update only the triangular factor
For new rows, the Gram identity becomes \[
X_{\mathrm{new}}^\top X_{\mathrm{new}}=X^\top X+UU^\top
=R^\top R+UU^\top.
\] rupdate() returns a new triangular factor satisfying this identity, without returning \(Q\). To delete those rows, rdowndate() takes their values in U rather than their positions.
For predictor insertion, the required cross-products have a different structure. Appending \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) gives \[
[X,V]^\top[X,V]
=\begin{pmatrix}R^\top R&X^\top V\\V^\top X&V^\top V\end{pmatrix}.
\] The old factor determines the upper-left block, but it does not contain the cross-products between X and the new predictors. This is why the R-only column-update interface also receives the design values. For row deletion, the values of the observations being removed determine the subtraction \(UU^\top\); their positions alone would not supply that information.
R_initial <- initial$R[seq_len(p), , drop = FALSE]
R_added <- fastQR::rupdate(X, R_initial, U = U, type = "row", fast = FALSE)
R_removed <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_added, U = U, type = "row", fast = FALSE)

# R-only column updates append new columns to the right.
R_wider <- fastQR::rupdate(X, R_initial, U = V, type = "column", fast = FALSE)
R_narrower <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_wider, k = p + 1L, m = ncol(V),
                               type = "column", fast = FALSE)
r_checks <- c(
  add_rows = relative_error(crossprod(R_added), crossprod(X_added)),
  remove_rows = relative_error(crossprod(R_removed), crossprod(X)),
  add_columns = relative_error(crossprod(R_wider), crossprod(cbind(X, V))),
  remove_columns = relative_error(crossprod(R_narrower), crossprod(X)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(operation = names(r_checks), error = r_checks),
             digits = 16, row.names = FALSE)



operation
error

4 A sliding-window regression
A moving window provides a statistical example of repeated updating and downdating. At each step we discard the oldest observation and append a new one. In addition to \(R\), we maintain \(h=X^\top y\). The regression coefficient vector solves \[
R^\top z=h,\qquad R\widehat\beta=z.
\] The first solve is lower triangular because it uses \(R^\top\); in R it is forwardsolve(t(R), h). The result is then passed to backsolve(R, ...). These are the two stages of solving \(R^\top R\widehat\beta=h\). Solving only \(R\widehat\beta=h\) would use a different system and would not recover the least-squares coefficients.
When one observation \((x_{\mathrm{old}}^\top,y_{\mathrm{old}})\) is removed and another is inserted, the response cross-product changes through \[
h_{\mathrm{new}}
=h_{\mathrm{old}}-x_{\mathrm{old}}y_{\mathrm{old}}
+x_{\mathrm{new}}y_{\mathrm{new}}.
\] Here each x on the right is a p-dimensional column vector. The code stores the corresponding design rows, so crossprod(old_x, old_y) and crossprod(new_x, new_y) construct these contributions in the required shape. Maintaining h makes the updated triangular factor usable for regression without recomputing the full response cross-product.
The simulation below keeps 100 observations in the window and processes 30 replacements. An intercept is included explicitly. At every step we compare the updated solution with a fresh lm.fit() fit.
set.seed(2028)
window <- 100L
steps <- 30L
p <- 5L
X_stream <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm((window + steps) * (p - 1L)),
                            window + steps, p - 1L))
beta_true <- c(1, 2, -1, 0, .5)
y_stream <- drop(X_stream %*% beta_true + rnorm(window + steps, sd = .7))
X_window <- X_stream[seq_len(window), , drop = FALSE]
y_window <- y_stream[seq_len(window)]
R_window <- fastQR::qr(X_window, complete = FALSE)$R
h <- crossprod(X_window, y_window)
coef_update <- coef_fresh <- matrix(NA_real_, steps, p)
gram_error <- numeric(steps)
for (s in seq_len(steps)) {
  old_x <- X_window[1, , drop = FALSE]
  old_y <- y_window[1]
  new_x <- X_stream[window + s, , drop = FALSE]
  new_y <- y_stream[window + s]
  R_minus <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_window, U = t(old_x), type = "row")
  X_minus <- X_window[-1, , drop = FALSE]
  R_window <- fastQR::rupdate(X_minus, R_minus, U = t(new_x), type = "row")
  h <- h - crossprod(old_x, old_y) + crossprod(new_x, new_y)
  X_window <- rbind(X_minus, new_x)
  y_window <- c(y_window[-1], new_y)
  coef_update[s, ] <- backsolve(R_window, forwardsolve(t(R_window), h))
  coef_fresh[s, ] <- lm.fit(X_window, y_window)$coefficients
  gram_error[s] <- relative_error(crossprod(R_window), crossprod(X_window))
}
max_coefficient_error <- max(abs(coef_update - coef_fresh))
stopifnot(max_coefficient_error < 1e-9, max(gram_error) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  check = c("Maximum coefficient difference", "Maximum relative Gram error"),
  value = c(max_coefficient_error, max(gram_error))), digits = 16)



check
value




Maximum coefficient difference
5.81e-14


Maximum relative Gram error
2.04e-14



The coefficient trajectories in Figure 1 show how the fitted model changes as observations enter and leave the window. Each updated trajectory is paired with a fresh least-squares fit on exactly the same observations. Their overlap checks the repeated-update calculation; variation along the horizontal axis reflects changes in the data window, rather than a different estimator.
path_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(step = rep(seq_len(steps), p), coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), each = steps)),
             estimate = as.vector(coef_update), method = "Updated factors"),
  data.frame(step = rep(seq_len(steps), p), coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), each = steps)),
             estimate = as.vector(coef_fresh), method = "Fresh fit"))
ggplot2::ggplot(path_data, ggplot2::aes(step, estimate, colour = coefficient,
                                      linetype = method)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Fresh fit" = "dashed", "Updated factors" = "solid")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Window replacement", y = "Coefficient estimate", colour = "Coefficient",
                linetype = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)





Figure 1: Coefficient estimates as the window advances. Solid lines use updated factors; dashed lines are fresh least-squares fits. The two computations agree to numerical precision.



Figure 1



This example illustrates the algorithm, not a claim about universal speed or long-run stability. Over long sequences, monitor reconstruction or Gram errors and consider periodic refactorization. Maintaining only \(R\) avoids storing \(Q\), but this particular example retains the data window so that observations can be deleted and reference fits checked.

title: Ridge regression as the design grows
text:
A sequence of ridge fits provides a useful setting in which to assess the value of updating a triangular factor. New observations change the information available about a fixed coefficient vector, whereas new predictors enlarge the model itself. Both operations can be represented as changes to an augmented least-squares design. This representation also allows us to consider more predictors than observations: a positive ridge penalty makes the augmented design full column rank even when the observed design is wide.
The comparison in this chapter concerns the numerical work required to fit the same specified model after a change in its design. We examine coefficient and prediction accuracy separately from elapsed time, and compare updating with a fresh LAPACK factorization of the augmented design. The penalty is specified in advance. Choosing it from the data is a separate procedure, discussed in the preceding chapter.

1 The augmented problem and the meaning of a fixed penalty
For a response matrix \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}\) and design \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), consider \[
\widehat B_\alpha=\arg\min_B\{\|Y-XB\|_F^2+\alpha\|B\|_F^2\},\qquad \alpha>0.
\] Writing \[
A_\alpha=\begin{bmatrix}X\\\sqrt\alpha I_p\end{bmatrix},\qquad
Y_\alpha=\begin{bmatrix}Y\\0_{p\times q}\end{bmatrix}
\] turns this criterion into an ordinary least-squares problem with a full-column-rank design. Indeed, for any nonzero vector \(v\), \[
v^\top A_\alpha^\top A_\alpha v=\|Xv\|_2^2+\alpha\|v\|_2^2>0.
\] This argument does not require \(p\le n\). If \(A_\alpha=QR\), then \[
R^\top R=X^\top X+\alpha I_p,\qquad
R^\top Z=X^\top Y,\qquad R\widehat B_\alpha=Z.
\] The last two equations describe an R-only workflow, which maintains the response cross-product as well as the factor. They are not interchangeable, in numerical accuracy, with explicitly applying the orthogonal transformations to \(Y_\alpha\). We therefore use the latter approach as an independent reference when checking the updated coefficients. The use of QR and augmented systems for least squares is discussed in Golub and Van Loan (2013) and Björck (2015).
The public ridge functions use the normalized criterion \(\|Y-XB\|_F^2/n+\lambda\|B\|_F^2\), so the parameter in the augmented design is \(\alpha=n\lambda\). Holding \(\alpha\) fixed while adding observations consequently changes the equivalent normalized parameter to \(\lambda_{n+m}=\alpha/(n+m)\). Holding \(\lambda\) fixed instead changes the total penalty. We treat these two experiments separately rather than silently changing the optimization problem.


2 A reproducible fit with more predictors than observations
The following example has forty observations and eighty predictors. A positive penalty gives a unique fit, despite the rank deficiency of the unpenalized problem. The two public interfaces are compared with a QR solve of the augmented design, whose right-hand side is transformed orthogonally.
set.seed(312)
n_wide <- 40L
p_wide <- 80L
X_wide <- matrix(rnorm(n_wide * p_wide), n_wide, p_wide)
y_wide <- rnorm(n_wide)
alpha_wide <- 8
lambda_wide <- alpha_wide / n_wide
wide_QR <- fastQR::qrridge(y_wide, X_wide, lambda_wide, type = "QR")
wide_R <- fastQR::qrridge(y_wide, X_wide, lambda_wide, type = "R")
A_wide <- rbind(X_wide, sqrt(alpha_wide) * diag(p_wide))
f_wide <- fastQR::qr_lapack(A_wide, output = "thin")
beta_reference <- backsolve(
  f_wide$R, crossprod(f_wide$Q, c(y_wide, rep(0, p_wide))))
c(QR_error = max(abs(wide_QR$coeff - beta_reference)),
  R_error = max(abs(wide_R$coeff - beta_reference)))
##     QR_error      R_error 
## 1.137979e-15 5.273559e-16
stopifnot(max(abs(wide_QR$coeff - beta_reference)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(wide_R$coeff - beta_reference)) < 1e-10)
The legacy residual diagnostic \(n-p\) is not a degrees-of-freedom formula for ridge regression. The updated interfaces return NA for this diagnostic and its associated variance estimates when \(p>n\); the coefficients, fitted values and requested predictions remain available. Effective ridge degrees of freedom are obtained from the smoother matrix, as explained in the preceding chapter. A zero penalty still requires full column rank, and therefore cannot be used to obtain a unique wide-design fit through these interfaces.


3 Adding observations
Suppose that \(U\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}\) contains new observations and \(V\in\mathbb R^{m\times q}\) their responses. At fixed \(\alpha\), the maintained quantities satisfy \[
R_{\rm new}^\top R_{\rm new}=R^\top R+U^\top U,
\qquad H_{\rm new}=H+U^\top V,\qquad H=X^\top Y.
\] The existing row-update routine applies to the augmented design. The penalty rows need not be added again: they are already represented in \(R\).
set.seed(313)
new_X <- matrix(rnorm(5L * p_wide), 5L, p_wide)
new_y <- rnorm(5L)
R_before <- fastQR::qr_lapack(A_wide, output = "R")
H_before <- crossprod(X_wide, y_wide)
R_after <- fastQR::rupdate(A_wide, R_before, U = t(new_X),
                          type = "row", fast = FALSE)
H_after <- H_before + crossprod(new_X, new_y)
beta_after <- backsolve(R_after, forwardsolve(t(R_after), H_after))
fit_after <- fastQR::qrridge(c(y_wide, new_y), rbind(X_wide, new_X),
                            lambda = alpha_wide / (n_wide + 5L), type = "R")
stopifnot(max(abs(beta_after - fit_after$coeff)) < 1e-10)
If the normalized parameter \(\lambda\) must remain fixed, the required identity is instead \[
R_{\rm new}^\top R_{\rm new}
=R^\top R+U^\top U+m\lambda I_p.
\] One valid construction appends both the observation rows and the additional penalty rows \(\sqrt{m\lambda}I_p\). This construction is exact, but its extra work can erase an advantage for updating. The timing comparison below includes this cost; a fixed-\(\alpha\) result must not be presented as evidence of a fixed-\(\lambda\) speedup.


4 Adding predictors
Let \(W\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) contain new predictors. With the same penalty on every coefficient, the enlarged augmented design can be arranged as \[
\begin{bmatrix}
X&W\\\sqrt\alpha I_p&0\\0&\sqrt\alpha I_k
\end{bmatrix}.
\] The first \(p\) columns are the old augmented design with \(k\) zero rows appended. Their triangular factor is still \(R\). The new columns have observation part \(W\), zeros on the old penalty rows, and their own diagonal penalty block. Updating these columns therefore includes the penalty on the new coefficients; appending \(W\) alone would solve a different problem.
set.seed(314)
k_new <- 3L
W_new <- matrix(rnorm(n_wide * k_new), n_wide, k_new)
A_padded <- rbind(A_wide, matrix(0, k_new, p_wide))
W_augmented <- rbind(W_new, matrix(0, p_wide, k_new),
                     sqrt(alpha_wide) * diag(k_new))
R_enlarged <- fastQR::rupdate(A_padded, R_before, U = W_augmented,
                             type = "column", fast = FALSE)
H_enlarged <- rbind(H_before, crossprod(W_new, y_wide))
beta_enlarged <- backsolve(R_enlarged,
                           forwardsolve(t(R_enlarged), H_enlarged))
fit_enlarged <- fastQR::qrridge(y_wide, cbind(X_wide, W_new),
                               lambda_wide, type = "R")
stopifnot(max(abs(beta_enlarged - fit_enlarged$coeff)) < 1e-10)
This column update includes a triangular solve whose accuracy depends on conditioning. The positive penalty separates the augmented columns from exact linear dependence, but does not provide a uniform accuracy guarantee for arbitrarily small penalties. The tests below use a moderate specified penalty and report the observed errors against an orthogonal reference.


5 Accuracy and time for the same updated fit
The experiments use tall and wide observed designs, two response variables, batches of ten observations or five predictors, and five calibrated timed repetitions after warm-up. Both timed workflows return coefficients through an R-only solve. The update starts from existing factors and a cached response cross-product; the alternative rebuilds the augmented factor and response cross-product. Construction of the augmented matrices needed by each workflow and the final triangular solves are included. Random-data generation, validation and initial factorization are excluded from these single-change measurements. The reference uses LAPACK without pivoting in both cases.

The difference between the two row experiments is part of the computational question. An observation update at fixed total penalty modifies only the data contribution, whereas retaining a fixed normalized penalty also modifies the regularization block. Likewise, a predictor update must introduce the new penalty directions. The measured comparison, including these operations, determines whether maintaining the factor is advantageous on a particular problem. The complete repetitions and validation values are saved with the guide rather than replaced by a universal speed claim.


6 Following the design across the boundary \(p=n\)
A sequence of changes tests whether errors accumulate in ways that a single update can conceal. One experiment adds predictors to a design with one hundred observations, increasing its width from sixty to one hundred and sixty columns. A second adds observations to a design with one hundred predictors, increasing its sample size from sixty to one hundred and sixty. Both hold \(\alpha=20\) fixed and cross the unpenalized boundary \(p=n\), while their augmented designs remain full column rank throughout.
Figure 8 displays the cumulative numerical work along each sequence. The same initial factorization cost is included in both curves. These path measurements are single elapsed-time trajectories, whereas the preceding table uses repeated calibrated calls. Small elapsed-time differences along the paths should therefore be read cautiously.
ridge_time_plot <- rbind(
 transform(ridge_path, method = "Updating", milliseconds = 1000 * update_cumulative),
 transform(ridge_path, method = "Recomputing", milliseconds = 1000 * recompute_cumulative))
ggplot2::ggplot(ridge_time_plot,
 ggplot2::aes(step, milliseconds, colour = method)) +
 ggplot2::geom_line() + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.5) +
 ggplot2::facet_wrap(~operation, scales = "free_y") +
 ggplot2::labs(x = "Update step", y = "Cumulative milliseconds", colour = NULL) +
 ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
 ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")





Figure 8: Cumulative elapsed time while adding observations or predictors at fixed total penalty. Both workflows include their initial factorization. Each panel shows one growing-design trajectory, rather than repeated timing estimates.

Figure 9 compares the updated coefficients and predictions with a fresh orthogonal reference at every step. Agreement across the transition through \(p=n\) checks the augmented construction; it does not imply that an unpenalized wide-design problem has become identifiable.
ridge_error_plot <- rbind(
 transform(ridge_path, quantity = "Coefficients", error = coefficient_error),
 transform(ridge_path, quantity = "Predictions", error = prediction_error))
ggplot2::ggplot(ridge_error_plot,
 ggplot2::aes(step, pmax(error, .Machine$double.eps), colour = quantity)) +
 ggplot2::geom_line() + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1.5) +
 ggplot2::scale_y_log10() + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~operation) +
 ggplot2::labs(x = "Update step", y = "Scaled error (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
 ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
 ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")





Figure 9: Coefficient and prediction errors along the growing-design sequences. Each reference is recomputed from the current augmented design by QR and orthogonal transformation of the response. Values below machine precision are clipped only for logarithmic display.



Figure 2



The paths show how the factor and response information can be reused through a changing statistical model. They do not include selecting the penalty, and their times do not include evaluating predictions over a separate large test set. The distinction between maintaining numerical information and choosing a model is essential when using these examples to motivate a statistical application.

Golub, Gene H., and Charles F. Van Loan. 2013. Matrix Computations. Fourth. Johns Hopkins Studies in the Mathematical Sciences. Johns Hopkins University Press, Baltimore, MD.

title: Least squares, ridge paths and model selection
text:
The factors become statistically useful when they are connected to an estimation problem and to the predictions obtained from its solution. This chapter begins with ordinary least squares, where a coefficient vector can be checked against an independent QR fit, and then introduces ridge regularization. A ridge path shows how the estimates change with the penalty; cross-validation supplies a separate procedure for choosing among those candidate fits.
The construction of the design remains part of the model specification. These matrix interfaces do not insert an intercept or perform preprocessing automatically, so the examples make those choices explicit. Both ridge backends are checked against augmented-design QR calculations, allowing differences in model specification to be distinguished from differences between numerical implementations.

title: Least squares, ridge paths and model selection
text:
2.1 The two numerical routes
In the QR backend, define \(A_\lambda=X^\top X/n+\lambda I_p\) and \(h=X^\top y\). The routine factorizes \(A_\lambda=Q_A R_A\), forms \(Q_A^\top h/n\) and solves the upper triangular system with \(R_A\). The factorization is therefore of the normalized penalized system, rather than of X itself.
The R backend uses the augmented design \(\widetilde X=[X^\top,\sqrt{n\lambda}I_p]^\top\) to obtain a triangular factor \(\widetilde R\) satisfying \(\widetilde R^\top\widetilde R=X^\top X+n\lambda I_p\). The coefficients follow from \[
\widetilde R^\top c=h,\qquad
\widetilde R\widehat\beta_\lambda=c.
\] These routes have the same exact-arithmetic solution, while their intermediate factors have different meanings. The examples compare their coefficients with an independent augmented-design QR solve, rather than comparing their R entries as though they were the same factorization.
The factor n follows from normalizing the data loss by the number of observations. Replicating all observations leaves this criterion, and therefore the estimate at a fixed penalty, unchanged. In a validation fold the same convention uses the number of training observations, not the size of the full dataset.

title: Least squares, ridge paths and model selection
text:
2.2 Centering, scaling and coefficient interpretation
Here lambda is a scalar. We build a path by calling the function once per grid value. All supplied columns are penalized. To leave the intercept unpenalized, center the response and predictors, estimate the slopes, and reconstruct the intercept. We also scale predictors using training-set standard deviations so that a common penalty has a comparable interpretation across columns.
Let \(\bar x_j\) and \(s_j\) denote the training mean and standard deviation of predictor j, and define \(Z_{ij}=(X_{ij}-\bar x_j)/s_j\). Fitting the centered response on Z produces standardized coefficients \(\widehat\gamma_\lambda\). The original-scale slopes and intercept are recovered through \[
\widehat\beta_{\lambda,j}=\widehat\gamma_{\lambda,j}/s_j,
\qquad
\widehat\alpha_\lambda=\bar y-\sum_j\bar x_j\widehat\beta_{\lambda,j}.
\] Thus a new prediction can be obtained either from the standardized design with the training means and scales, or from the original predictors with these recovered coefficients. The penalty acts on the standardized coefficients, which is why changing predictor units without an explicit scaling convention can change the fit.
x_mean <- colMeans(X)
x_scale <- apply(X, 2, sd)
y_mean <- mean(y)
Z <- sweep(sweep(X, 2, x_mean, "-"), 2, x_scale, "/")
y_centered <- y - y_mean
lambda <- exp(seq(log(1e-4), log(10), length.out = 50L))
path_standardized <- vapply(lambda, function(lam) {
  as.numeric(fastQR::qrridge(y_centered, Z, lambda = lam, type = "QR")$coeff)
}, numeric(p))
path_triangular <- vapply(lambda, function(lam) {
  as.numeric(fastQR::qrridge(y_centered, Z, lambda = lam, type = "R")$coeff)
}, numeric(p))
stopifnot(max(abs(path_standardized - path_triangular)) < 1e-10)
path_slopes <- sweep(path_standardized, 1, x_scale, "/")
path_intercept <- y_mean - drop(crossprod(x_mean, path_slopes))

# Independent augmented-design QR calculation at one grid value.
j <- 20L
reference <- qr.coef(base::qr(rbind(Z, sqrt(n * lambda[j]) * diag(p))),
                     c(y_centered, rep(0, p)))
stopifnot(max(abs(path_standardized[, j] - reference)) < 1e-10)
The R-only calculation at one path value can also be checked directly from its returned triangular factor. The inner forwardsolve() reconstructs the response coordinates, and the following backsolve() returns the coefficients. The additional rows in the augmented QR reference contain zeros in the response because they encode only the penalty.
ridge_R_fit <- fastQR::qrridge(y_centered, Z, lambda[j], type = "R")
ridge_rhs <- crossprod(Z, y_centered)
ridge_coordinates <- forwardsolve(t(ridge_R_fit$R), ridge_rhs)
ridge_explicit <- backsolve(ridge_R_fit$R, ridge_coordinates)
ridge_manual_error <- max(abs(ridge_explicit - path_triangular[, j]))
stopifnot(ridge_manual_error < 1e-10)
Figure 3 follows the fitted slopes as the penalty increases. Expressing the coefficients on the original predictor scale makes their statistical interpretation consistent with the data-generating model, while the logarithmic penalty axis reveals changes across several orders of magnitude. Agreement between the two numerical backends is checked before the paths are drawn.
path_table <- data.frame(lambda = rep(lambda, each = p),
                         coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), length(lambda))),
                         estimate = as.vector(path_slopes))
ggplot2::ggplot(path_table, ggplot2::aes(lambda, estimate, colour = coefficient)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) + ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Coefficient estimate", colour = "Predictor") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)





Figure 3: Ridge slopes on their original predictor scale, plotted against a logarithmic penalty grid. The coefficients change continuously with the penalty; ridge does not generally create an exactly sparse fit.

title: fastQR
text:
Reading the guide
The Theory page derives the projection and triangular-solve calculations used throughout the examples. The decomposition chapter then connects those identities to the representations returned by R functions. Updating follows the factors through changes in the data, while regression introduces estimation, regularization and validation. The accuracy chapter revisits the same operations to distinguish the sensitivity of the problem from the numerical error and timing of a particular calculation.
The discussion assumes familiarity with vectors, matrix multiplication and elementary regression. Quantities introduced in the mathematics are connected to their dimensions and to the corresponding R expressions, so the code can be read as an implementation of the argument rather than as a sequence of unexplained function calls.

The LAPACK comparison reads the CSV files distributed in the benchmark archive. Unpack that archive into the project directory before running the complete example script.
Package authors: Mauro Bernardi, Claudio Busatto and Manuela Cattelan. Bibliographic details are provided in Further reading.
The tutorial Ridge with growing designs follows observation and predictor additions through the boundary between tall and wide designs. It compares maintained triangular factors with fresh LAPACK factorizations, and distinguishes a fixed total penalty from a fixed normalized penalty.
Ridge by marginal likelihood derives an empirical Bayes alternative to cross-validation: the coefficients are integrated out, the noise variance is profiled, and the penalty is estimated from the resulting response model. Reproducible simulations compare the selectors on both tall and wide designs.
The empirical Bayes R helpers and simulation driver are available separately, as well as in the complete guide project.

title: Numerical accuracy and reproducible timing
text:
A numerical method has to produce an adequate answer before its execution time becomes informative. For matrix factorizations, this involves checking both the identities satisfied by the returned factors and the accuracy of the calculations that use them. These checks address different parts of a statistical computation: reconstructing a design accurately does not, by itself, establish that its regression coefficients can be estimated accurately when the design is nearly singular.
The timing experiments therefore follow the numerical comparisons. Each experiment specifies the information available at its starting point and the representation required at its end. Compact Householder information, explicit thin factors and complete factors involve different amounts of computation and storage. Keeping those requests separate makes the measurements relevant to an actual choice of workflow.

title: Numerical accuracy and reproducible timing
text:
1.1 Computing the two coefficient estimates
For each design, fastQR::qr(X, complete = FALSE) returns \(Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) and \(R_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\). The direct QR estimate is obtained from \[
c=Q_1^\top y,\qquad R_1\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{QR}}=c.
\] The first operation expresses the response in the orthonormal basis. The second recovers its coefficients relative to the original design columns. The projection identity \[
\|y-Xb\|_2^2
=\|Q_1^\top y-R_1b\|_2^2+\|(I_n-Q_1Q_1^\top)y\|_2^2
\] shows why this solves the least-squares problem: the final term is independent of b, and the triangular solve makes the first term zero. In the code, crossprod(f$Q, y) computes c and backsolve(f$R, c) performs the backward substitution. The factor R has the same singular values as X, so this solve remains sensitive when the design is ill conditioned; using QR does not make that sensitivity disappear.
The normal-equation estimate is computed through a different numerical route, \[
A=X^\top X,\qquad h=X^\top y,\qquad
A\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{NE}}=h.
\] These equations define the same coefficient vector in exact arithmetic when X has full column rank. They are represented by solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)) in the experiment. Forming A explicitly introduces rounding into a system whose condition number is the square of that of X. The comparison therefore separates the sensitivity of the original coefficient problem from the additional effects of the computational route used to solve it.
set.seed(2032)
n <- 160L
p <- 12L
U <- qr.Q(base::qr(matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)))
V <- qr.Q(base::qr(matrix(rnorm(p * p), p, p)))
beta <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = p)
condition_numbers <- 10^(0:8)
accuracy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(condition_numbers, function(kappa_target) {
  singular_values <- exp(seq(0, -log(kappa_target), length.out = p))
  X <- sweep(U, 2, singular_values, "*") %*% t(V)
  y <- drop(X %*% beta)
  f <- fastQR::qr(X, complete = FALSE)
  projected_response <- crossprod(f$Q, y)  # p coordinates in the Q basis
  b_qr <- backsolve(f$R, projected_response) # solve R beta = Q' y
  b_normal <- tryCatch(solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)),
                        error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, p))
  data.frame(condition = kappa_target,
    reconstruction = norm(X - f$Q %*% f$R, "F") / norm(X, "F"),
    QR_coefficients = sqrt(sum((b_qr - beta)^2) / sum(beta^2)),
    normal_equations = sqrt(sum((b_normal - beta)^2) / sum(beta^2)))
}))

  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")





Figure 10: Relative reconstruction and coefficient errors versus the prescribed condition number. Missing normal-equation values indicate that the reference solver rejected the system as numerically singular.



Figure 1



For a full-column-rank design, \(\kappa_2(X^\top X)=\kappa_2(X)^2\). Thus a design with condition number \(10^8\) produces a cross-product matrix with condition number approximately \(10^{16}\), close to the reciprocal of double-precision machine accuracy. Rounding in the formation of the cross-products can then have a substantial effect, and a solver may reasonably treat the resulting system as numerically singular. Missing points on the normal-equation curve indicate such a rejection; they do not represent zero error.
The QR coefficient curve comes from the explicit projection and triangular solve displayed in the code. Its comparison with the reconstruction curve concerns these particular calculations, rather than every possible use of a QR representation. Values smaller than machine epsilon are placed at epsilon in the plot to keep the logarithmic display readable; the underlying numerical values remain in the table.

title: From a matrix to a verified QR factorization
text:
A design matrix often appears in several related calculations: estimating coefficients, producing predictions, adding observations or changing the set of predictors. A QR factorization records its geometry in a form that can support each of these operations. Understanding what the factors contain is therefore useful before deciding whether to store an explicit orthogonal basis, retain only a triangular factor or keep the orthogonal transformations in compact form.
This chapter introduces those representations through the identities they satisfy. The examples check reconstruction and orthogonality separately, then examine the column-ordering convention used by pivoted QR. These checks provide a common basis for the update and regression examples that follow.
The examples use fastQR 1.1.6, ggplot2 for figures and knitr for tables. All code uses explicit fastQR:: or base:: namespaces because both packages export a function named qr. For the examples in this guide, use the accompanying verified source build described on the Overview page. No attachment with library(fastQR) is required below.

title: From a matrix to a verified QR factorization
text:
1.1 Rank and rectangular shapes
The factorization identity itself does not require a unique least-squares coefficient vector. If a design has dependent columns, a triangular factor can still represent it, but solving an unpivoted triangular system with a zero diagonal is no longer the full-column-rank calculation derived above. A rank-revealing pivoted factorization separates that situation from an ordinary full-rank solve.
A wide design with \(p>n\) also admits an orthogonal factorization, with Q of size \(n\times n\) and R of size \(n\times p\). It cannot have full column rank, so its unpenalized coefficient vector is not uniquely determined by the fitted response. The qr() and compact qr_fast() interfaces support that representation; the thin-factor interface has a different input contract. Ordinary least-squares interfaces retain their full-column-rank restrictions. Positive-penalty ridge fits also support wide designs; the chapter on ridge with growing designs develops this case through augmented least squares.
The declared numerical rank and the number of stored Householder transformations also serve different purposes. Extraction through qr_Q() and qr_R() follows their documented rank-dependent output rule. qr_Q_full() constructs the complete orthogonal transformation from the compact information when that full transformation is required.

title: From a matrix to a verified QR factorization
text:
2.1 Recovering a least-squares coefficient vector
Once the thin factors are available, the response enters through its projection onto the columns of Q. For a response \(y\in\mathbb R^n\), define \(c=Q_1^\top y\). The least-squares coefficient vector satisfies \(R_1\widehat\beta=c\), so a complete calculation needs a matrix-vector product followed by a triangular solve. Writing \(R_1^{-1}c\) is a mathematical identity, but an implementation can obtain the result without constructing an inverse.
The following response combines a linear signal with a deterministic perturbation. The perturbation makes the residual nonzero, allowing us to check its orthogonality to the fitted column space as well as the coefficient calculation. It is a numerical example, rather than a simulation of a particular observation-noise model.
demo_y <- drop(X %*% seq_len(p)) + sin(seq_len(n))
demo_projection <- crossprod(thin$Q, demo_y)
demo_coefficients <- backsolve(thin$R, demo_projection)
demo_fitted <- drop(X %*% demo_coefficients)
demo_residuals <- demo_y - demo_fitted
qr_derivation_checks <- c(
  coefficient_agreement = max(abs(demo_coefficients - lm.fit(X, demo_y)$coefficients)),
  fitted_projection = relative_error(demo_fitted, thin$Q %*% demo_projection),
  residual_orthogonality = max(abs(crossprod(thin$Q, demo_residuals))) /
    max(1, sqrt(sum(demo_y^2))))
stopifnot(max(qr_derivation_checks) < 1e-10)

                        error = unname(qr_derivation_checks)), digits = 12)

The response projection has p entries, whereas the fitted response and residual have n. Multiplication by the thin Q maps between those coordinate systems. The near-zero value of \(Q_1^\top e\) verifies the defining least-squares geometry, while comparison with lm.fit() checks the resulting coefficients against a separate implementation.

title: Choose the function for your task
text: This is a task-oriented guide, not a replacement for help() in the installed package. The tutorials validate the particular code paths shown with fastQR 1.1.6.

title: Choose the function for your task
text:
1 Reading an interface in context
A function name identifies an interface, but the matrix being factorized and the information returned still depend on the task. An explicit decomposition of X supplies factors that reconstruct that design. A compact decomposition stores transformations defining the orthogonal factor. A regression routine uses such calculations within a model-fitting procedure and can return factors of a working system instead of the original design.
This distinction is particularly relevant for ridge. With type = "QR", the returned Q and R factorize the normalized penalized system. With type = "R", the triangular factor comes from an augmented design and satisfies a different cross-product identity. The coefficient vectors solve the same normalized ridge problem, but their intermediate factors should not be interchanged as though they described the same matrix.

text:
2 Decomposition and extraction

Purpose

Obtain a triangular Gram factor



For a tall design, the upper triangular part of the leading square block in qr_fast() output contains R. Entries below the diagonal store Householder-vector information, while qraux stores the corresponding transformation coefficients. Those entries are part of a compact representation, rather than a reconstruction error left below the triangle. The extraction helpers interpret that storage and apply the transformations when explicit factors are needed.
The decomposition tutorial explains the permutation convention. Use fastQR::qr() and base::qr() explicitly when comparing implementations.

For row batches, the examples supply a p by m matrix, with each new observation stored in a column. QR insertion uses a one-based position. R-only insertion of predictors appends columns to the right.
The orientation follows the algebra. A batch of new observations contributes U %*% t(U) to the predictor cross-product matrix, whereas new predictor columns require cross-products with the existing observations. For an R-only row deletion, the values of the removed observations are supplied because their contributions must be subtracted. For a QR deletion by position, the current complete factors also encode the relevant observation geometry. These are different input conventions for related matrix operations.

text:
4 Solve and estimate

4.1 Orthogonal transformations and coefficient coordinates
The products returned by qr_Qty() and qr_Qy() use the complete orthogonal transformation encoded by the compact factors. Their input vector has n entries, and their output also has n entries. For a tall full-column-rank design, the first p coordinates of the complete transformed response agree with the thin projection crossprod(Q1, y). A subsequent triangular solve is still required to obtain p regression coefficients.
The qr_lse_Qty() and qr_lse_Qy() helpers construct the factorization internally and apply the corresponding complete transformation. This separates multiplication by an orthogonal factor from projection onto a fitted column space: the least-squares fitted response uses both stages, Q1 transpose followed by Q1, while a coefficient vector uses the projection followed by the triangular solve. Keeping track of those dimensions makes the similarly named operations easier to distinguish.


4.2 Model specification and validation
The model-fitting functions receive numeric designs rather than formula objects. A column of ones must be supplied when an intercept is part of the design, and ridge penalizes that column unless the intercept is handled separately by centering. A fixed-penalty fit and a validation procedure are also different operations: the first estimates coefficients at a supplied value, while the second compares held-out prediction losses and then refits at a selected value.
Prediction designs must reproduce the training column definitions and ordering. When preprocessing is estimated from data, the transformation used for a validation observation must be learned from its training fold; the transformation for a final test prediction is learned from the complete training sample. The explicit validation loop illustrates these distinctions before the native CV interfaces are introduced.


4.3 Scope of the regression examples
The regression chapter checks both ridge backends and the univariate and multivariate cross-validation interfaces against independent augmented-design QR calculations. It also retains an explicit fold loop for examples that estimate centering and scaling within each training fold. These procedures have different preprocessing and intercept conventions; the distinction is explained before the native CV example.
help("qrupdate", package = "fastQR")
help("qrridge", package = "fastQR")
The positive-penalty ridge interfaces, including cross-validation, also accept more predictors than observations. See Ridge with growing designs for augmented-design updates and the distinction between fixed total and normalized penalties. Ordinary least-squares interfaces retain their full-column-rank restrictions.

title: Choosing the ridge penalty by marginal likelihood
text:
Cross-validation selects a penalty by measuring predictive performance on observations omitted from fitting. A probability model offers another route: the coefficient vector can be integrated out, leaving a marginal likelihood for the regularization parameter. This chapter develops that construction explicitly, including the normalization terms that would be lost by treating a penalized residual sum of squares as a likelihood on its own.
We first describe the Gaussian model and derive its marginal likelihood, then explain how the variance and penalty are estimated. The implementation uses a single singular value decomposition to avoid repeating a matrix factorization at every candidate penalty. An independent QR calculation verifies the resulting coefficients. The concluding simulations compare this empirical Bayes procedure with an efficient cross-validation calculation on both tall and wide designs, under a dense Gaussian signal and a sparse signal that departs from the assumed coefficient distribution.
Gaussian marginal likelihood and hyperparameter selection are treated in Rasmussen and Williams (2006), Chapters 2 and 5. For work specifically on fast marginal likelihood selection of ridge parameters using singular values, see Karabatsos (2015). The construction below fixes its own prior and profiles the noise variance; it should not be read as a reproduction of every prior or algorithm in those references.

title: Choosing the ridge penalty by marginal likelihood
section: 3.1 The score equation and the conditional smoother trace
text:
3.1 The score equation and the conditional smoother trace
The singular values also give an interpretable derivative of the profile criterion. With \(t=\log\lambda\) and \(\alpha=n\exp(t)\), define \[
\dot q_\alpha=\sum_{j=1}^r z_j^2
\frac{\alpha d_j^2}{(d_j^2+\alpha)^2},\qquad
d_\alpha=\sum_{j=1}^r\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+\alpha}.
\] Differentiating the profile criterion gives \[
\frac{\mathrm d F}{\mathrm d t}
=\frac12\left(\frac{n\dot q_\alpha}{q_\alpha}-d_\alpha\right).
\] Here \(d_\alpha\) is the trace of the ridge smoother at a fixed penalty. An interior empirical Bayes optimum balances these two terms. This identity is useful for checking an optimizer, but it does not justify replacing the marginal-model variance estimate \(q_\alpha/n\) with a residual degrees-of-freedom adjustment. The numerical checks below compare the analytic derivative with a centered finite difference.

title: Mathematical background and further reading
text:
The computational ideas in this guide build on standard orthogonal factorizations and their modification after changes to a matrix. For full treatments, see Golub and Van Loan (2013) and Björck (2015); for least-squares algorithms, see Björck (2024). The package authors develop updating methods and statistical applications in Bernardi, Busatto, and Cattelan (2024).

1 Why orthogonal transformations?
Consider the full-column-rank least-squares problem \[
\widehat\beta=\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb R^p}\|y-Xb\|_2^2,
\qquad X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p},\quad y\in\mathbb R^n,\quad n\ge p.
\] The thin factorization \(X=Q_1R_1\) separates an orthonormal basis \(Q_1\) for the column space from the coordinates stored in the triangular matrix \(R_1\). Complete that basis to \(Q=[Q_1,Q_2]\), so that \(Q^\top Q=I_n\). Orthogonal multiplication preserves Euclidean length, and \[
Q^\top(y-Xb)
=\begin{pmatrix}Q_1^\top y-R_1b\\Q_2^\top y\end{pmatrix}.
\] Taking squared lengths gives \[
\|y-Xb\|_2^2
=\|Q_1^\top y-R_1b\|_2^2+\|Q_2^\top y\|_2^2.
\] The second term is unchanged when \(b\) changes. Because \(R_1\) is nonsingular, the first term can be made zero by solving \[
c=Q_1^\top y\in\mathbb R^p,
\qquad R_1\widehat\beta=c.
\] These are the two computational stages of a direct QR least-squares solve: project the response onto the orthonormal basis, then recover its coordinates relative to the original columns of \(X\). In R, the projection is crossprod(Q1, y) and the triangular solution is backsolve(R1, c). No inverse of \(R_1\) is formed.
The triangular structure determines the order of the solve. The last equation gives \(\widehat\beta_p=c_p/r_{pp}\); the preceding equations are recovered backwards through \[
\widehat\beta_j
=\frac{c_j-\sum_{k=j+1}^p r_{jk}\widehat\beta_k}{r_{jj}},
\qquad j=p-1,\ldots,1.
\] The nonzero diagonal entries required here follow from full column rank. The fitted response and residual are \[
\widehat y=Q_1Q_1^\top y,
\qquad e=y-\widehat y=(I_n-Q_1Q_1^\top)y.
\] Thus \(Q_1^\top e=0\): the residual is orthogonal to every direction used to construct the fit. This identity supplies a useful numerical check in addition to agreement between coefficient vectors.
If only \(R_1\) and \(h=X^\top y\) are retained, the same coefficients follow from \(R_1^\top R_1\widehat\beta=h\). The calculation then requires a forward solve followed by a backward solve, \[
R_1^\top z=h,\qquad R_1\widehat\beta=z.
\] In exact arithmetic, \(z=Q_1^\top y\), since \(X^\top y=R_1^\top Q_1^\top y\). This relation explains why an R-only representation can support regression, and why the right-hand side has to be maintained alongside the factor. The numerical consequences of forming cross-products are examined in the accuracy chapter (Golub and Van Loan 2013; Björck 2024).


2 Classical and modified Gram–Schmidt
Let \(X=[x_1,\ldots,x_p]\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) have linearly independent columns, with \(n\geq p\). Classical Gram–Schmidt constructs an orthonormal basis for their span. At step \(k\), set \[
\begin{aligned}
r_{jk}&=q_j^\top x_k\quad(j<k),\\
v_k&=x_k-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}r_{jk}q_j,\\
r_{kk}&=\|v_k\|_2,\qquad q_k=v_k/r_{kk}.
\end{aligned}
\] The empty sum at \(k=1\) is zero. Full column rank ensures \(r_{kk}>0\) in exact arithmetic. With \(r_{jk}=0\) for \(j>k\), these identities give \(X=QR\) and \(Q^\top Q=I_p\). The temporary residual \(v_k\) is distinct from the normalized vector \(q_k\).
Modified Gram–Schmidt instead starts with \(v=x_k\) and, for \(j=1,\ldots,k-1\), successively computes \[
r_{jk}=q_j^\top v,\qquad v\leftarrow v-r_{jk}q_j;
\] it then sets \(r_{kk}=\|v\|_2\) and \(q_k=v/r_{kk}\). The two algorithms are equivalent in exact arithmetic, but their floating-point behavior differs: computing projections from the updated residual generally reduces loss of orthogonality. Reorthogonalization may still be needed for difficult problems (Golub and Van Loan 2013; Björck 2015).
At each step, the inner products describe the part of the current column already explained by the existing basis. Subtracting those components leaves a residual direction; normalizing that residual supplies the next basis vector. The recorded coefficients give the identity \(x_k=\sum_{j\le k}q_jr_{jk}\), so the construction produces both factors rather than Q alone.
The following educational implementation follows the modified scheme. Its diagonal check detects a residual that is too small relative to the input column to normalize reliably. That check is useful for understanding the algorithm, but it is not a general rank-revealing procedure. The example checks reconstruction and orthogonality separately on a well-conditioned design.
mgs <- function(X) {
  n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X)
  Q <- matrix(0, n, p); R <- matrix(0, p, p)
  for (k in seq_len(p)) {
    v <- X[, k]
    if (k > 1L) for (j in seq_len(k - 1L)) {
      R[j, k] <- sum(Q[, j] * v)
      v <- v - R[j, k] * Q[, j]
    }
    R[k, k] <- sqrt(sum(v^2))
    if (R[k, k] <= .Machine$double.eps * sqrt(sum(X[, k]^2)))
      stop("Numerically dependent column: use a rank-revealing factorization.")
    Q[, k] <- v / R[k, k]
  }
  list(Q = Q, R = R)
}
set.seed(2040)
X_gs <- matrix(rnorm(80 * 8), 80, 8)
gs <- mgs(X_gs)
gs_checks <- c(reconstruction = norm(X_gs - gs$Q %*% gs$R, "F") / norm(X_gs, "F"),
               orthogonality = norm(crossprod(gs$Q) - diag(8), "F"))
gs_checks
## reconstruction  orthogonality 
##   1.154784e-16   1.019128e-15
stopifnot(max(gs_checks) < 1e-10)


3 Householder transformations and Givens rotations
Gram–Schmidt constructs basis vectors by successive projections. Householder QR instead transforms the matrix into triangular form using reflections. For a nonzero vector \(v\), the matrix \[
H=I-2vv^\top/(v^\top v)
\] is symmetric and satisfies \(H^\top H=I\). For a column segment \(x\), a reflector can be chosen so that \(Hx=\alpha e_1\), eliminating every entry of that segment except its first. Applying such a transformation to successive trailing submatrices removes the entries below the diagonal without changing Euclidean lengths.
If the embedded reflections satisfy \(H_s\cdots H_1X=R\), then \[
X=QR,\qquad Q=H_1\cdots H_s,
\] with the full or thin factors selected as required. Each reflection is represented by a vector and a coefficient, so its action can be applied without storing a dense matrix H. Compact Householder output retains that information. Forming Q, multiplying by Q and multiplying by its transpose are related operations, but need not incur the same storage cost.
A Givens rotation acts on just two coordinates. With \[
G=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix},\qquad c^2+s^2=1,
\] choosing \(c=a/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) and \(s=b/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) gives \[
G\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\\0\end{pmatrix}
\] when \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\). Implementations compute the rotation parameters with appropriate numerical safeguards. Because a rotation changes only a pair of coordinates, a sequence of rotations can restore triangular form after a local insertion or deletion.
Both constructions use orthogonal transformations to control the propagation of rounding error. They do not remove sensitivity already present in a nearly singular design. The distinction between an accurate factorization and an accurate coefficient vector is therefore retained throughout the numerical experiments (Golub and Van Loan 2013; Björck 2015).


4 What a row update changes
Suppose \(X=Q_1R_1\) has already been computed and a batch of \(m\) observations is represented by \(U^\top\), where \(U\in\mathbb R^{p\times m}\). The enlarged design is \[
X_+=\begin{pmatrix}X\\U^\top\end{pmatrix}.
\] Applying the previously available orthogonal transformation to the original observation block reduces the new factorization problem to triangularizing \[
\begin{pmatrix}R_1\\U^\top\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^{(p+m)\times p},
\] together with zero rows that do not affect the triangular factor. The new observations have to be incorporated, but the original n-row design need not be factorized again to obtain R.
The corresponding cross-product identity is \[
X_+^\top X_+=R_1^\top R_1+UU^\top.
\] It also explains what additional information a regression update needs. If \(y_+\) is the vector of responses for the new batch, the right-hand side becomes \(h_+=h+Uy_+\), where \(h=X^\top y\). Updating R alone does not update that response-dependent quantity.
Deleting observations reverses the signs in both updates. The resulting cross-product matrix is positive semidefinite when the deleted rows belong to the original design; it is positive definite precisely when the remaining design has full column rank. A downdated factor may still represent a rank-deficient design, but the unpivoted triangular coefficient solve then requires further treatment. Near a loss of rank, cancellation in the subtraction makes the numerical checks especially important.


5 Ridge as augmented least squares
For the normalized ridge criterion used in the regression chapter, define the augmented response and design by \[
\widetilde y=\begin{pmatrix}y\\0_p\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{n+p},\qquad
\widetilde X=\begin{pmatrix}X\\\sqrt{n\lambda}I_p\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^{(n+p)\times p}.
\] The \(p\) additional entries of \(\widetilde y\) are zero, and the \(p\) additional rows of \(\widetilde X\) encode the penalty. For \(b\in\mathbb R^p\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\widetilde y-\widetilde Xb\|_2^2
&=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}y-Xb\\-\sqrt{n\lambda}b\end{pmatrix}\right\|_2^2\\
&=\|y-Xb\|_2^2+n\lambda\|b\|_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\] Multiplying the normalized criterion by n does not change its minimizer, so the ridge estimate is the ordinary least-squares solution for these augmented data. With a thin factorization \(\widetilde X=\widetilde Q_1\widetilde R_1\), it can be computed by \[
\widetilde R_1\widehat\beta_\lambda
=\widetilde Q_1^\top\widetilde y.
\] Equivalently, differentiating the original criterion gives \[
(X^\top X+n\lambda I_p)\widehat\beta_\lambda=X^\top y.
\] The extra rows imply \(\widetilde R_1^\top\widetilde R_1=X^\top X+n\lambda I_p\). An R-only calculation therefore uses this factor in two triangular solves, just as in the unpenalized case. A positive penalty makes the system positive definite even when X has dependent columns, although a particular fitting interface can impose additional restrictions on input dimensions.
The augmented formulation is an independent way to check the implementations. It also identifies the scale of the penalty: the factor n is a consequence of dividing the data loss by n. Within cross-validation, n is replaced by the size of the corresponding training set.
The intercept is handled separately in the ridge tutorial by centering. If a column of ones were simply included in the penalized design, that coefficient would also be penalized. Predictor means and scales must be estimated again within each cross-validation training fold.


6 Choosing a representation
The representation should retain the information needed by the next calculation. A compact factorization stores the transformations defining Q and is useful when only their action on vectors is required. Thin factors make the column-space basis explicit, supporting projections and direct QR solves. A full factorization also retains an orthogonal complement, which is used by some update routines but can require substantially more storage for a tall design.
An R-only representation is sufficient when subsequent operations need the cross-product information \(R^\top R\) and triangular solves. Regression still requires a compatible right-hand side such as \(X^\top y\), and insertion of new predictors can require cross-products with their observed values. These requirements distinguish the information needed by the algorithm from the matrix finally returned to R.
The examples use reconstruction identities, independent coefficient calculations and recorded timings to examine those choices. The function guide describes the interfaces, while the numerical experiments show how representation, conditioning and the starting information affect the computation.
